offers.text: My partner keeps saying chatbots are conscious and I want ammunition to argue back.

rows.answer:
For a debate, read three places closely and skim the rest.

Start with the split between intelligence and consciousness. Your partner may be treating them as one thing [spya-nj888h spya-j0a9rq]. The essay also says our habits push us to read chatbots as conscious [spya-cqh2pq].

Next, the central argument is that simulating something isn't the same as being it: "A simulation of a rainstorm does not make anything actually wet" [spya-npjt4j]. It's easy to repeat in an argument.

Last, the author admits he could be wrong [spya-qu7j89]. Concede that point and your case sounds more credible.

Quotes will pull out the lines worth repeating.

rows.answer:
Start with the section on why we're tempted. Seth argues that intelligence and consciousness are different things [spya-nj888h], and that language is especially good at fooling us [spya-k6fpme]. That answers "but it talks like it has feelings."

Next, read the "simulation is not instantiation" section. Its rainstorm line is the easiest to repeat in an argument [spya-npjt4j].

Be careful with one point. Seth admits he "might be wrong" [spya-qu7j89] and says nobody can be sure either way [spya-zajp75]. If you claim certainty, your partner can point to that.
